comm.t: Medhas, still speaking to King Suratha and the merchant Samādhi, begins the second story: the Goddess’s war with Mahiṣāsura and his armies. This uvāca opens the middle carita (Madhyama Carita), which runs from chapter 2 to chapter 4.

In the Gita Press pāṭha the middle carita has its own viniyoga and dhyāna, recited before this mantra: Viṣṇu is named its ṛṣi, Mahālakṣmī its deity, uṣṇik its metre, Śākambharī its śakti and Durgā its bīja. This is liturgical tradition, not part of the Purāṇa. The bījas ॐ ह्रीं that open the mantra in recitation belong to the same pāṭha.

samasa.alt: It can also be taken as a samāhāra dvandva (neuter singular) in loose apposition to युद्धम्. The regular adjective of relation would be दैवासुर (with vṛddhi); the Purāṇas use the bare dvandva in the stock phrase देवासुरं युद्धम्, and the attributive reading fits the agreement with युद्धम्.

mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause (देवासुरं युद्धम् अभूत्, with पूर्णम् अब्दशतम् for its length) comes first; two locative absolutes name the leaders on each side.
mantras.lit: Long ago there was a war of gods and asuras for a full hundred years, Mahiṣa being lord of the asuras and Purandara of the gods.
mantras.tr: Long ago the gods and the asuras fought for a full hundred years, when Mahiṣa was lord of the asuras and Indra lord of the gods.
mantras.tr_note: Purandara is rendered by the familiar name Indra in tr.

comm.t: The second story opens like the first, with a time and a conflict: a hundred-year war, with Mahiṣa leading the asuras and Indra the gods. The first pāda of the second line is one syllable too long (nine, not eight) in every witness; the text is left as it is.

Mahiṣa means ‘buffalo’; the asura’s buffalo form appears in chapter 3, where he fights the Goddess in that shape and in others. The tradition calls the Goddess of this carita Mahiṣāsuramardinī, ‘crusher of the buffalo-asura’.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a passive one (देवसैन्यं पराजितम्, agent in the instrumental) and an active one with an absolutive (जित्वा … महिषासुरः इन्द्रः अभूत्).
mantras.lit: There the army of the gods was defeated by the asuras of great valour; and having conquered all the gods, Mahiṣāsura became Indra.
mantras.tr: In that war the mighty asuras routed the army of the gods; and having conquered every god, Mahiṣāsura made himself Indra.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Made himself Indra’ renders इन्द्रः अभूत् ‘became Indra’, i.e. took Indra’s place as king of heaven.

comm.t: The war ends in the gods’ defeat, and Mahiṣa takes Indra’s place. ‘Indra’ here is an office: lordship over heaven, which the victor seizes.

The gods’ complaint (2.6) spells out what the usurpation means: Mahiṣa occupies the offices (अधिकारान्) of the Sun, Fire, Wind, Moon, Yama and Varuṇa as well as Indra’s. Cosmic functions in the Purāṇas are posts held by gods, and here they have been taken over by a single asura.

mantras.lit: Then the defeated gods, placing at their head the lotus-born Prajāpati, went there where the Lord and the Garuḍa-bannered one were.
mantras.tr: Then the defeated gods, with Brahmā the lotus-born creator at their head, went to where Śiva and Viṣṇu were.
mantras.tr_note: ईश and गरुडध्वज are rendered by the names Śiva and Viṣṇu; ‘were’ is supplied.

comm.t: The gods go to the two great gods with Brahmā at their head. This is the usual Purāṇic pattern: when the lesser gods are defeated, they seek the higher powers.

All three gods of the trimūrti are present. The Goddess who appears will come from their tejas first (2.10) and then from that of all the others (2.11). In the first carita Brahmā alone praised her; here all the gods together bring her forth.

mantras.lit: The Thirty related to those two, just as it happened, the doings of Mahiṣāsura and likewise the full account of the gods’ humiliation.
mantras.tr: The gods told the two of them everything Mahiṣāsura had done, exactly as it happened, and the whole story of their own defeat.

comm.t: The gods report to Śiva and Viṣṇu. The next three verses (2.6–8) give their report in their own words.

The gods here are called ‘the Thirty’ (त्रिदशाः), a common name of the gods in epic and Purāṇic Sanskrit. The text gives Mahiṣa’s offence twice: first in the narrator’s summary (2.3), then from the gods’ side as humiliation (अभिभव).

अधिकार (अधि + √कृ + घञ्) is ‘authority, office, function’: the share of the world’s working that belongs to each god.

mantras.lit: Of the Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind and Moon, of Yama and Varuṇa, and of the others, the offices he himself alone occupies.
mantras.tr: He has seized for himself the offices of the Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind and Moon, of Yama and Varuṇa, and of the other gods besides.
mantras.tr_note: tr puts the verb first and renders the present ‘occupies’ as ‘has seized’, which is its sense here.

comm.t: The gods’ speech to Śiva and Viṣṇu begins here (2.6–8). Mahiṣa has not only taken Indra’s throne (2.3); he has taken over every god’s function himself.

The list reads as an inventory of the cosmos: light (Sun), rule (Indra), sacrifice (Agni), breath (Wind), the waters (Varuṇa), death (Yama), the moon. When one asura holds them all, the order of the world is in the hands of its enemy. The Goddess who answers this will receive gifts from these very gods (2.20–31).

mantras.lit: Driven out of heaven by him, by the evil-minded Mahiṣa, all the hosts of gods wander on the earth like mortals.
mantras.tr: Cast out of heaven by that wicked Mahiṣa, all the gods now wander the earth like mortal men.

comm.t: The second part of the complaint: the gods are exiles, wandering the earth like humans. The gods’ condition now matches Suratha’s, who also lost his kingdom and wandered alone (1.6–11).
A modern reading: the text lets even the gods lose their place. Being dispossessed is not a mark of unworthiness here; it is the condition from which help is sought.

Past participle of प्र + √पद् with active sense (a verb of motion): ‘having approached’. शरणं प्रपद् is the fixed idiom ‘to go to (someone) for refuge’, with the person in the accusative.
Passive imperative (third person): ‘let his death be thought out’. A polite way to put a request to superiors.

mantras.anvaya: एतत् सर्वम् अमरारिविचेष्टितं वः कथितम्। वः शरणं प्रपन्नाः स्मः। तस्य वधः विचिन्त्यताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three short clauses: a passive statement (कथितम्), an active one (प्रपन्नाः स्मः) and a passive request (विचिन्त्यताम्).
mantras.lit: This, all the doings of the enemy of the immortals, has been told to you. We have come to you for refuge; let his killing be devised.
mantras.tr: We have told you all that the enemy of the gods has done. We have come to you for refuge: find a way to destroy him.
mantras.tr_note: tr turns the two passives into active English.

comm.t: The gods end their report and ask for help: they take refuge with the high gods and ask them to plan Mahiṣa’s death. They do not ask the gods to fight; they ask them to think (विचिन्त्यताम्). What answers is not a plan but anger, and from the anger the Goddess comes (2.9–13).

शरणं प्रपद् ‘to go for refuge’ is the language of surrender (prapatti). Here the gods take refuge with Śiva and Viṣṇu; later the same language is turned to the Goddess herself: she is शरण्या ‘the refuge’ in the Nārāyaṇī hymn (11.10, 11.12), and Medhas ends by telling the king to go to her for refuge (13.4, तामुपैहि महाराज शरणं परमेश्वरीम्).

mantras.lit: Having heard thus the words of the gods, Madhusūdana grew angry, and Śambhu, both with faces twisted by frowning brows.
mantras.tr: Hearing the gods speak in this way, Viṣṇu and Śiva grew angry, their faces dark with frowning brows.
mantras.tr_note: tr uses the names Viṣṇu and Śiva for Madhusūdana and Śambhu.

comm.t: The response to the gods’ appeal is anger, not counsel. Viṣṇu is called Madhusūdana, a reminder of his victory over Madhu in the first carita, a victory won only when the Goddess released him from sleep.

A modern reading: the text makes anger the starting point of the manifestation. It is the anger of the powerful at the suffering of the worlds, and the Goddess who takes form from it is the answer to that suffering.

mantras.lit: Then, from the face of the discus-bearer, filled with intense anger, from there, came forth a great radiance, and from Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
mantras.tr: Then from the face of Viṣṇu, the bearer of the discus, burning with anger, a great radiance came forth, and from the faces of Brahmā and Śiva as well.
mantras.tr_note: The second ततः is absorbed into ‘from’; ‘the faces’ is supplied for Brahmā and Śiva.

comm.t: The tejas of the three great gods comes first, out of their faces, in their anger. Viṣṇu is named first and his anger is stressed (अतिकोप).

Tejas is more than light: it is the fiery power and splendour that belongs to a god. Each god’s share of it is given a part of the Goddess’s body in 2.14–18, beginning with Śiva’s (the face) and Viṣṇu’s (the arms).

flags.uncertain: The second ततः (end of the first line) is read as ‘from there’, reinforcing वदनात्. It can also be taken as a resumptive ‘then’, filling the line; the sense is the same.

mantras.anvaya: अन्येषां च एव शक्रादीनां देवानां शरीरतः सुमहत् तेजः निर्गतम्। तत् च ऐक्यं समगच्छत।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the tejas came out (निर्गतम्, participle as verb), and it merged (समगच्छत).
mantras.lit: And from the bodies of the other gods too, Śakra and the rest, came out a very great radiance; and that came together into oneness.
mantras.tr: From the bodies of the other gods as well, Indra and the rest, a great radiance poured forth, and all of it came together and became one.

comm.t: After the three great gods, all the others give their tejas, and it all merges. The Goddess will not be the tejas of any one god but of all of them together.

The gods’ hymn in chapter 4 says this outright: the Goddess’s form is the gathered power of all the hosts of gods (4.3, निश्शेषदेवगणशक्तिसमूहमूर्त्या). The tradition reads this as the unity of the divine powers, which the gods could not achieve as separate beings but she embodies.

mantras.lit: Those gods saw there an immense mass of radiance, like a blazing mountain, whose flames filled the space of the quarters.
mantras.tr: There the gods saw a vast mass of light like a mountain on fire, its flames filling every direction.

comm.t: Before it takes a form, the merged tejas is seen as a burning mountain that fills space. The gods are spectators of what they have given.
A modern reading: what the gods could not do apart becomes visible when their powers are pooled. The image is of overwhelming, undirected force, waiting for a form.

Aorist of √भू with a predicate nominative: तत् … नारी अभूत्, ‘it became a woman’. The neuter subject and the feminine predicate stand side by side: the transformation is in the grammar.

mantras.anvaya: तत्र सर्वदेवशरीरजम् अतुलं तत् तेजः एकस्थं (सत्), त्विषा व्याप्तलोकत्रयं तत् नारी अभूत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A neuter subject (तत् तेजः, resumed by the second तत्) with its qualifiers, a feminine predicate (नारी) and the verb अभूत्.
mantras.lit: There that matchless radiance, born from the bodies of all the gods, gathered into one, which had pervaded the three worlds with its brilliance, became a woman.
mantras.tr: There that matchless radiance, born from the bodies of all the gods, gathered into one place and, filling the three worlds with its light, became a woman.
mantras.tr_note: tr keeps व्याप्तलोकत्रयम् with the radiance, as the neuter requires, but turns it into a participial phrase.

comm.t: The central moment of the chapter: the combined tejas becomes a woman. The verse is carefully neuter until the last noun: it is the radiance (तेजः, n.) that is matchless, gathered and world-filling, and that radiance ‘became a woman’ (नारी अभूत्).

Medhas has already said that the Goddess is eternal and is called ‘born’ only when she becomes manifest for the gods’ purpose (1.64–66: देवानां कार्यसिद्ध्यर्थमाविर्भवति सा यदा). The tradition therefore reads this verse as a manifestation, not a creation: the gods’ tejas gives her a visible form; it does not bring her into being.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) opens with a similar emergence: name 4, चिदग्निकुण्डसम्भूता, ‘she who arose from the fire-pit of consciousness’, and name 5, देवकार्यसमुद्यता, ‘she who is intent on the gods’ purpose’. There she rises from a sacrificial fire, here from the gods’ combined tejas; the two accounts are distinct.

mantras.lit: The radiance that was Śambhu’s — by that her face was formed; and by Yama’s the hair came to be; the arms by the radiance of Viṣṇu.
mantras.tr: From Śiva’s radiance her face was formed; from Yama’s, her hair; from Viṣṇu’s, her arms.
mantras.tr_note: tr compresses the relative construction (यत् … तेन) into a simple ‘from’.

comm.t: The second movement begins: each god’s tejas forms one part of the woman’s body (2.14–18). Śiva gives the face, Yama the hair, Viṣṇu the arms.

A modern reading: the pairings invite reflection (the arms that will hold the weapons from Viṣṇu the preserver, the dark hair from Yama, lord of death), but the text itself states only the correspondence and gives no reasons.

mantras.anvaya: सौम्येन (तेजसा) स्तनयोः युग्मम् (अभवत्), ऐन्द्रेण च मध्यम् अभवत्, वारुणेन च जङ्घोरू (अभवताम्), भुवः तेजसा नितम्बः (अभवत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four parallel clauses, each with the source in the instrumental and the body part as subject; अभवत् is stated once and understood in the rest.
mantras.lit: By Soma’s (radiance) the pair of breasts, and by Indra’s the waist came to be; and by Varuṇa’s the shanks and thighs; the hips by the radiance of the Earth.
mantras.tr: From the Moon’s radiance her breasts were formed, from Indra’s her waist, from Varuṇa’s her legs, and from the Earth’s radiance her hips.

comm.t: The forming of the body continues: breasts from Soma, waist from Indra, legs from Varuṇa, hips from the Earth. The givers include the Earth, a goddess, alongside the gods.

The Purāṇa describes the Goddess’s body plainly, part by part, and the passage is recited as it stands. Its point is that no part of her is the gift of a single deity: she is assembled from the whole pantheon, the Earth included.

mantras.lit: By the radiance of Brahmā the feet, their toes by the radiance of the Sun; and by the Vasus’ the fingers, and by Kubera’s the nose.
mantras.tr: From Brahmā’s radiance came her feet, from the Sun’s her toes, from the Vasus’ her fingers, and from Kubera’s her nose.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Came’ is supplied; the verse has no verb of its own.

comm.t: The list continues. Brahmā, the creator, gives the feet; the Sun the toes; the Vasus the fingers; Kubera, lord of wealth, the nose. The verse has no verb: the pattern of 2.14–15 carries it.

Brahmā, who led the gods to Śiva and Viṣṇu (2.4), gives the Goddess her feet. The tradition makes much of the Goddess’s feet as the place of refuge and worship, and here the creator’s own tejas forms them.

mantras.lit: Her teeth came into being by the radiance of Prajāpati; likewise the triad of eyes was born by the radiance of Fire.
mantras.tr: Her teeth were formed from the radiance of Prajāpati, and her three eyes, likewise, from the radiance of Fire.

comm.t: The teeth come from Prajāpati’s tejas and the three eyes from Agni’s. The Goddess has three eyes, like Śiva.
Three eyes are a mark the Goddess shares with Śiva, whose third eye is traditionally the eye of fire. Here all three of her eyes are formed from Agni’s tejas.

flags.uncertain: प्राजापत्येन तेजसा: which Prajāpati is meant is not stated. Since Brahmā’s tejas has already given the feet (2.16), the Prajāpati here is probably another (one of the lords of creatures, such as Dakṣa) or the Prajāpatis as a class; it is translated simply as ‘Prajāpati’. The reading itself is not in doubt.

mantras.anvaya: भ्रुवौ च संध्ययोः तेजः, श्रवणौ च अनिलस्य (तेजः)। अन्येषां च एव देवानां तेजसां सम्भवः शिवा (अभूत्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal sentences of the form ‘X (was) Y’s radiance’, then a summary sentence with शिवा as subject and सम्भवः as predicate.
mantras.lit: And the brows (were) the radiance of the two Twilights, and the ears (that) of the Wind; and Śivā was the issue of the radiances of the other gods as well.
mantras.tr: Her brows were the radiance of the two Twilights, her ears that of the Wind; and so the auspicious Goddess arose from the radiance of all the other gods as well.
mantras.tr_note: tr renders सम्भवः … शिवा as ‘the auspicious Goddess arose from’.

comm.t: The description ends with a summary: the rest of the gods contributed too, and the being who arose from all their radiance is called Śivā, ‘the auspicious’. The two Twilights (संध्ये, dawn and dusk) are counted among the givers.

Śivā is the feminine of śiva, ‘auspicious, benign’, and a name of the Goddess as Śiva’s consort. This is the first time the text uses it: the being formed from anger-born radiance is named ‘the auspicious one’.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name, शिवा (name 53), and श्रीशिवा (name 998). The name is common to many Śākta texts; the two works are distinct.

mantras.lit: Then, having beheld her, who had arisen from the mass of radiance of all the gods, the immortals, oppressed by Mahiṣa, attained joy.
mantras.tr: Then the gods, so long oppressed by Mahiṣa, looked on her who had arisen from the gathered radiance of them all, and they were filled with joy.

comm.t: The gods see the woman formed from their pooled tejas and rejoice. Their joy closes the account of her birth and opens the giving of gifts (2.20–31).
A modern reading: the gods rejoice at something greater than any of them, which is also their own power given back in a new form.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel sentences: giver, an absolutive phrase (how the weapon was made), the gift, and the verb.
mantras.lit: Drawing out a trident from (his own) trident, the bearer of Pināka gave it to her; and Kṛṣṇa, producing a discus from his own discus, gave it.
mantras.tr: Śiva, bearer of the Pināka bow, drew a trident out of his own trident and gave it to her; and Viṣṇu brought forth a discus from his own discus and gave it to her.
mantras.tr_note: tr names the givers Śiva and Viṣṇu for पिनाकधृक् and कृष्ण, and repeats ‘to her’.

comm.t: The gifts begin. Each weapon is drawn out of the god’s own weapon: the gods do not give theirs away but make a second one from it. Śiva gives the trident and Viṣṇu the discus.

The dhyāna of the middle carita in the Gita Press pāṭha (recited before 2.1) pictures Mahālakṣmī holding these gifts: trident, discus (सुदर्शन), conch, spear, bow, thunderbolt, bell, staff, noose, rosary, water-pot, sword and shield among them. The chapter supplies the story behind that iconography.

flags.uncertain: Kṛṣṇa here is a name of Viṣṇu (the discus-bearer of 2.10), not specifically the avatāra. पिनाकधृक्: the final member -धृक् ‘holding’ is common at the end of compounds; its derivation (from √धृ, or by analogy with forms of √धृष्) is not certain. GRETIL’s Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa carries additional verse material at this point (recension note in corrections.json); the Gita Press text is followed.

mantras.lit: Indra, lord of the immortals, producing a thunderbolt from (his own) thunderbolt, gave it to her, the thousand-eyed one, and a bell from the elephant Airāvata.
mantras.tr: Indra, the thousand-eyed lord of the gods, brought forth a thunderbolt from his own and gave it to her, together with a bell from his elephant Airāvata.

comm.t: Indra gives a thunderbolt made from his own and the bell of his elephant Airāvata. The god whose throne Mahiṣa took is named by his full titles: lord of the immortals, the thousand-eyed.

mantras.anvaya_en: Four gifts in two lines; ददौ is stated twice and understood with the other two givers.
mantras.lit: Yama (gave) a staff from (his) staff of death, and the lord of the waters gave a noose; and Prajāpati gave a rosary; Brahmā a water-pot.
mantras.tr: Yama gave her a staff drawn from his own staff of death, and Varuṇa, lord of the waters, a noose; Prajāpati gave her a rosary, and Brahmā a water-pot.

comm.t: Yama gives a staff, Varuṇa a noose (his second gift, after the conch in 2.21), Prajāpati a rosary and Brahmā a water-pot. The last two are not weapons but the emblems of an ascetic and of the creator.
The noose (पाश) is Varuṇa’s ancient emblem, the bond with which he binds wrongdoers. In the battle the Goddess will use it to bind asuras and drag them along (2.57, पाशेन बद्ध्वा).

flags.uncertain: प्रजापतिश्चाक्षमालां ददौ ब्रह्मा कमण्डलुम्: with ददौ stated twice, the verse is taken as naming two givers, Prajāpati (as in 2.17, distinct from Brahmā) and Brahmā. It can also be read as one giver, ‘Brahmā the Prajāpati gave a rosary and a water-pot’, since Brahmā is called प्रजापति in 2.4. The reading itself is not in doubt.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line has no verb of its own (ददौ from 2.23 is understood); the second is a full sentence with two objects.
mantras.lit: Into all the pores (of her skin) the Day-maker (set) his own rays; and Kāla gave her a sword and a spotless shield.
mantras.tr: The Sun filled every pore of her body with his own rays, and Time gave her a sword and a gleaming shield.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Filled’ is supplied for the missing verb of the first line.

comm.t: The Sun’s gift is not a weapon but his light, set into every pore of her skin: the Goddess shines from within. Kāla, Time, gives the sword and shield.
Kāla here is Time personified, a power that ends all things, and so a fitting giver of the sword. The sword and shield are among the weapons named in the dhyāna of the middle carita (असिं च चर्म).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess सर्वायुधधरा, ‘bearer of all weapons’ (name 530). In the Devī Māhātmya the same idea is told as a story: every weapon she holds was given to her by a god.

flags.uncertain: The first line has no finite verb; ददौ (or a verb of placing) is understood. Kāla is taken as Time personified, distinct from Yama (2.23), who is named separately.

samasa.alt: Also analysed as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, क्षीरस्य उदः ‘the water of milk’, i.e. the milk-sea; the bahuvrīhi suits a personified giver. उद stands for उदक as the final member of such compounds.

samasa.sense: a jewel worn on the crown of the head
samasa.alt: Also saptamī tatpuruṣa, चूडायां मणिः ‘the jewel (worn) on the crest’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Neuter dual of an a-stem (nom./acc. -e): ‘two garments’, the upper and the lower cloth. With अजरे it is a pair of everlasting robes.
Neuter dual again: earrings come as a pair, so the dual is the natural number. A dual in -e is pragṛhya, but here both duals stand before consonants, so no hiatus arises.

mantras.anvaya: क्षीरोदः च अमलं हारम्, अजरे अम्बरे च, तथा दिव्यं चूडामणिम्, कुण्डले कटकानि च (ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The verse has a subject and a string of objects but no verb of its own; ददौ, the verb of the whole catalogue (2.20–31), is supplied. The list of ornaments runs on into 2.26 and 2.27a.
mantras.lit: And the Milk-Ocean (gave) a spotless necklace and likewise two unaging garments, likewise a divine crest-jewel, two earrings and bracelets,
mantras.tr: The Ocean of Milk gave her a spotless necklace, a pair of garments that never wear out, a heavenly crest-jewel, earrings and bracelets,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Gave her’ is supplied from the catalogue’s verb ददौ; the sentence continues into 2.26–27.

comm.t: After the weapons come the ornaments. The Ocean of Milk, the store of treasures in Purāṇic myth, dresses the newly formed Goddess: necklace, a pair of imperishable garments, crest-jewel, earrings and bracelets. The verse names a giver but no verb; the list continues for a verse and a half.

Where the list of the Ocean’s gifts ends is not marked. The usual reading lets it run to the finger-rings of 2.27a, so that Viśvakarman’s gift begins with the axe; others give the jewellery after the garments to the craftsman Viśvakarman, whose verb ददौ follows in 2.27. The Sanskrit allows both.

flags.uncertain: The verse has no verb, and the boundary between the Ocean’s gifts and Viśvakarman’s (2.27) is not marked in the text; the translation follows the common reading (the Ocean gives everything to the rings of 2.27a).

mantras.lit: likewise a bright half-moon, armlets on all the arms, likewise two spotless anklets, an unsurpassed neck-ornament,
mantras.tr: a gleaming crescent, armlets for all her arms, a pair of shining anklets and a peerless collar,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues from 2.25 and into 2.27.

comm.t: The list of ornaments continues from head to foot: a crescent for the head, armlets for ‘all her arms’, anklets and a collar. The plural arms anticipate 2.39, where she fills the directions with a thousand arms.

The same ornament vocabulary describes the Goddess’s form in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): 31, कनकाङ्गदकेयूरकमनीयभुजान्विता (arms lovely with golden aṅgadas and keyūras), and 32, रत्नग्रैवेयचिन्ताकलोलमुक्ताफलान्विता (with a jewelled graiveya and pearls). This is a shared iconographic vocabulary, not a borrowing between the two texts.

mantras.lit: the Ocean gave to her, and an exceedingly beautiful lotus. Himavat (gave) a lion as mount, and various jewels.
mantras.tr: the Ocean gave her, with a lotus of surpassing beauty. Himavat gave her a lion to ride, and jewels of every kind.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Gave’ is supplied for Himavat.

Himavat is, in Purāṇic tradition, the father of Pārvatī; here the mountain simply gives what belongs to the mountains — the lion and its jewels. The lion-mount gives her the name सिंहवाहिनी in 2.34.

morph.note: A litotes: ‘not empty of wine’ means ‘always full’. The thing it is not empty of is in the instrumental (सुरया).
Accusative, though it stands beside the nominatives शेषः … सर्वनागेशः: it anticipates नागहारम्, the object in the next verse.

mantras.anvaya: धनाधिपः सुरया अशून्यं पानपात्रं ददौ। सर्वनागेशः शेषः च महामणिविभूषितं (नागहारं तस्यै ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second line begins a sentence finished in 2.31: Śeṣa is its subject, and the accusative adjective waits for its noun नागहारम्.
mantras.lit: The Lord of Wealth gave a drinking-cup never empty of wine. And Śeṣa, the lord of all serpents, (gave) a … adorned with great jewels
mantras.tr: Kubera, Lord of Wealth, gave her a drinking-cup never empty of wine; and Śeṣa, king of all serpents, a jewel-studded
mantras.tr_note: The second line runs into 2.31, where the noun (नागहारम्) and the verb stand.

comm.t: Kubera, keeper of the gods’ treasure, gives a cup that is never empty of wine. The cup returns in battle: before slaying Mahiṣa she drinks and says ‘Roar, roar for a moment, fool, while I drink the honey-wine’ (3.38).

The wine-vessel is among the eighteen objects of the madhyama-carita dhyāna (सुराभाजनम्, Gita Press pāṭha). In the Śākta tradition the cup is commonly read as the Goddess’s exhilaration in battle, not as an ordinary indulgence; the text itself says only what is given.

The nominative here is the subject of the next verse’s सम्मानिता … ननाद; the instrumentals सुरैः, भूषणैः, आयुधैः are the agent and the means of that participle.

mantras.anvaya: यः इमां पृथिवीं धत्ते, (सः शेषः) तस्यै नागहारं ददौ। अन्यैः अपि सुरैः भूषणैः तथा आयुधैः देवी (सम्मानिता)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the sentence begun in 2.30 with a relative clause on Śeṣa. The second line opens a new sentence whose participle and verb (सम्मानिता … ननाद) stand in 2.32.
mantras.lit: serpent-necklace he gave to her — he who bears this earth. By other gods too, with ornaments and with weapons likewise, the Goddess —
mantras.tr: serpent-necklace — Śeṣa, who bears this earth. And the Goddess, honoured by the other gods as well with ornaments and weapons,
mantras.tr_note: The second line is completed by सम्मानिता in 2.32; ‘honoured’ is brought forward for English order.

comm.t: Śeṣa, the serpent who holds up the earth, gives a jewelled serpent-necklace. Then the list is closed with a summary: the other gods too honoured her with ornaments and weapons.

Śākta readers see in the catalogue of gifts (2.20–31) the gods handing back to the Goddess powers that are hers: several weapons are drawn out of the gods’ own weapons (2.20–23), as her body was drawn out of their light (2.13–18).

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the first finishes 2.31b (देवी … सम्मानिता ननाद); the second is passive, with the roar as agent.
mantras.lit: honoured, roared loudly with loud laughter again and again. By her terrible roar the whole sky was filled.
mantras.tr: roared aloud again and again, with peals of laughter. The whole sky was filled with her terrible roar.

comm.t: Armed and adorned, the Goddess’s first act is a roar mixed with laughter. The roar fills the sky; the next two verses follow its effect through the worlds.
Her laughter in the face of battle is a recurring mark of this carita: she fights without effort and is unwearied (अनायस्तानना, 2.50). Laughter here shows sovereignty, not mockery.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses: the echo caused by the roar (instrumental of cause), the worlds shaken, the seas trembling.
mantras.lit: By the uncontainable, exceedingly great (roar) a mighty echo arose. All the worlds were shaken, and the oceans trembled.
mantras.tr: From that boundless, immense roar a mighty echo rang out; all the worlds were shaken and the oceans trembled.

comm.t: The roar is too great to be held anywhere; its echo sets the worlds and oceans shaking. The effects are listed outward: sky (2.32), worlds and seas (2.33), earth and mountains (2.34).
The roar is the first sign the asuras receive of her: it is this sound that Mahiṣa rushes towards in 2.37 (अभ्यधावत तं शब्दम्).

flags.uncertain: अमायता is taken as the instrumental of a negated present participle (‘uncontainable’). The same letters can be divided अमायत अतिमहता, with अमायत an imperfect ātmanepada of √मा (‘it was measured / contained’); but that leaves the clause without a negative and without a clear subject, so the participle reading is followed.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses of upheaval, then the gods’ acclamation: ‘जय’ इति is the quoted word, ताम् the person addressed.
mantras.lit: The earth shook, and all the mountains quaked. And the gods with joy said ‘Be victorious!’ to her, the lion-rider.
mantras.tr: The earth shook and all the mountains quaked, and the gods cried out in joy to the lion-rider, ‘Victory to you!’
mantras.tr_note: ‘Victory to you’ renders the imperative जय (‘be victorious’).

comm.t: The roar reaches the earth and the mountains, and the gods answer it with one word: जय. सिंहवाहिनी is the first epithet the gods give her after her arming.

जय, ‘be victorious’, is at once an acclamation and a prayer. The same imperative is the refrain of the Argalā Stotra recited before the text in the Gita Press pāṭha (जय त्वं देवि चामुण्डे …), a separate liturgical hymn.

mantras.anvaya: भक्तिनम्रात्ममूर्तयः मुनयः च एनां तुष्टुवुः। अमरारयः समस्तं त्रैलोक्यं संक्षुब्धं दृष्ट्वा (2.36: सन्नद्धाखिलसैन्याः समुत्तस्थुः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the scene of praise. The second line starts a new sentence: the absolutive clause with its subject अमरारयः, whose main verb comes in 2.36.
mantras.lit: And the sages, their own bodies bowed with devotion, praised her. Having seen the whole three worlds agitated, the enemies of the immortals —
mantras.tr: The sages, bowing low in devotion, sang her praise. But the enemies of the gods, seeing the three worlds in turmoil,
mantras.tr_note: ‘But’ marks the change of scene, which the Sanskrit makes by a new subject; the sentence continues into 2.36.

comm.t: Two answers to the roar. The sages praise her with bowed bodies; the asuras, seeing the worlds in upheaval, prepare for war (2.36). The same event is heard as grace by the one side and as threat by the other.
A modern reflection: the verse sets reverence and alarm side by side as responses to one and the same power. What a person sees in an upheaval says something about where they stand.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 2.35b. The second gives Mahiṣāsura’s cry, quoted with इति, as an absolutive clause; his main verb is in 2.37.
mantras.lit: they, their entire armies armed, rose up with weapons raised. Having exclaimed in anger, ‘Ah! What is this?’, Mahiṣāsura —
mantras.tr: rose up, weapons raised, their whole army in arms. ‘Ha! What is this?’ cried Mahiṣāsura in fury,
mantras.tr_note: The absolutive आभाष्य (‘having exclaimed’) is rendered as a finite verb; the sentence runs on into 2.37.

comm.t: The asuras arm themselves, and Mahiṣāsura appears in the narrative for the first time in person, with an angry question: ‘What is this?’ He does not yet know what the sound is.

A modern reading: Mahiṣa meets the Goddess first as a disturbance to be put down — ‘What is this?’ — not as a power to be understood. The question is asked in anger, and anger does not wait for the answer.

mantras.tr: and charged towards the sound with all his asuras around him. Then he saw the Goddess, her radiance filling the three worlds,
mantras.tr_note: The second sentence continues through 2.38 into 2.39a, all describing the Goddess as he sees her.

mantras.anvaya: (सः) पादाक्रान्त्या नतभुवं, किरीटोल्लिखिताम्बरां, धनुर्ज्यानिःस्वनेन क्षोभिताशेषपातालां तां (देवीं ददर्श)।
mantras.anvaya_en: All accusatives in apposition to देवीम् (2.37); each bahuvrīhi has its own instrumental of cause beside it.
mantras.lit: her by whose tread the earth was bowed, by whose crown the sky was scraped, by the twang of whose bowstring all the netherworlds were shaken —
mantras.tr: the earth bending beneath her tread, her crown grazing the sky, the twang of her bowstring shaking the underworlds to their depths,
mantras.tr_note: The verse continues the object of ददर्श (2.37); the next verse completes it.

comm.t: What Mahiṣa sees is the Goddess as large as the cosmos: her foot presses the earth, her crown touches the sky, and the sound of her bow reaches the netherworlds. The three levels of the world are each touched by her.

Purāṇic cosmology divides the world into the heavens above, the earth, and the pātālas below. The verse touches all three, so that before a blow is struck the asura sees that the one he means to fight is as wide as the world.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the description of the Goddess (object of ददर्श, 2.37). The second line is a new sentence; तया देव्या is the instrumental of the one fought against (सह is understood).
mantras.lit: standing, having pervaded the directions on every side with a thousand arms. Then the battle of the enemies of the gods with that Goddess began,
mantras.tr: standing with her thousand arms spread through every quarter. Then the battle began between the Goddess and the enemies of the gods,
mantras.tr_note: The second line continues into 2.40, which describes the battle.

comm.t: The vision is completed by her arms, a thousand of them, filling the directions; then the battle begins. ‘A thousand’ here means beyond counting, completing the vertical vastness of 2.38 with the horizontal.

The madhyama-carita dhyāna of the Gita Press pāṭha pictures Mahālakṣmī with eighteen objects in her hands; the text’s own vision here is of a thousand arms. The two do not compete: the dhyāna is a form for meditation, the verse a vision of her cosmic extent.

mantras.anvaya: (तत् युद्धं) बहुधा मुक्तैः शस्त्रास्त्रैः आदीपितदिगन्तरम् (आसीत्)। महिषासुरसेनानीः चिक्षुराख्यः महासुरः (2.41: युयुधे)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line qualifies युद्धम् (2.39). The second introduces Cikṣura, the subject of युयुधे at the head of 2.41.
mantras.lit: (a battle) in which the spaces between the quarters were lit up by weapons and missiles discharged in many ways. Mahiṣāsura’s general, the great asura named Cikṣura,
mantras.tr: a battle in which the weapons and missiles they hurled set the whole horizon ablaze. Cikṣura, the mighty asura, Mahiṣāsura’s commander,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence of the second line is completed by युयुधे in 2.41.

comm.t: The battle is first seen as a whole — the horizon lit by weapons — and then its leaders are named one by one, beginning with Cikṣura, Mahiṣa’s commander. He is the first to attack the Goddess in chapter 3 (3.2).

From here to 2.47 the text gives a muster-roll of Mahiṣa’s generals with the size of their forces. Most of them are killed by name in chapter 3: Cikṣura (3.2ff.), Cāmara (3.11–16), Udagra (3.17), Bāṣkala (3.18), Mahāhanu (3.19), Biḍāla (3.20).

mantras.anvaya_en: युयुधे closes the sentence of 2.40b and is understood again with Cāmara. The second line names Udagra, whose verb is अयुध्यत at the head of 2.42.
mantras.lit: fought; and Cāmara, with others, accompanied by an army of four divisions. The great asura named Udagra, with six ten-thousands of chariots,
mantras.tr: joined battle; so did Cāmara, with others and an army of all four arms. Udagra, the mighty asura, with sixty thousand chariots,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Sixty thousand’ renders षड्भिः अयुतैः (six ayutas). The second line continues into 2.42.

comm.t: The first three generals: Cikṣura, Cāmara with a full army, and Udagra with sixty thousand chariots. The fourfold army (चतुरङ्ग) is the classical Indian army of elephants, chariots, horse and foot.
The numbers grow as the roll goes on — tens of thousands, then millions, then crores — to show the scale of what one Goddess faces. The point is the disproportion, not the arithmetic.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second introduces परिवारितः, taken as the name of the next general, whose verb is अयुध्यत in 2.44.
mantras.lit: With six hundreds of ten-thousands Bāṣkala fought in the battle. Parivārita, with many hosts of thousands of elephants and horses,
mantras.tr: Bāṣkala fought in the battle with six million. Parivārita, with many thousands of elephants and horses in their hosts,
mantras.tr_note: परिवारितः is rendered as a name (see Morph and Flags); ‘six million’ renders six hundred ayutas.

comm.t: Bāṣkala comes with six hundred ayutas — six million. He is struck down with a bhindipāla in 3.18, where the Gita Press prints the name as वाष्कल (b and v are interchangeable in many manuscripts).

Translators divide the next lines differently. Taking परिवारितः as a name gives each verb of 2.43–45 its own general (Bāṣkala, Parivārita, Biḍāla); taking it as ‘surrounded’ leaves Bāṣkala, or Biḍāla, as the subject of two verbs.

flags.uncertain: परिवारितः may be a proper name (Parivārita) or the participle ‘surrounded’; the name reading is followed because अयुध्यत in 2.44a has no other subject. No general of that name appears among those slain in chapter 3.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 2.43b (subject परिवारितः). The second introduces Biḍāla; his verb and the genitive रथानाम् stand in 2.45.
mantras.lit: and surrounded by a crore of chariots, fought in that battle. And the one named Biḍāla, with fifty of ten-thousands, and with ten-thousands —
mantras.tr: and a crore of chariots about him, fought in that battle. Biḍāla, with fifty ayutas
mantras.tr_note: The doubled ‘ayuta’ is rendered once (see Morph); ‘a crore’ is ten million. The sentence continues into 2.45.

comm.t: The general of 2.43b fights encircled by elephants, horses and a crore of chariots; then Biḍāla (‘Cat’) is named, with fifty ayutas — half a million — of chariots.
Biḍāla is beheaded by the Goddess’s sword in 3.20 (बिडालस्यासिना कायात्पातयामास वै शिरः).

flags.uncertain: अयुतानां … पञ्चाशद्भिः अथ अयुतैः repeats अयुत; the sense ‘fifty ayutas’ is adopted, but ‘fifty ayutas of ayutas’ is grammatically possible. The sandhi rules out a split into पञ्चाशद्भिः रथायुतैः.

mantras.tr: of chariots around him, fought in that battle. And other great asuras, each with chariots, elephants and horses by the ten thousand,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Great asuras’ is brought forward from 2.46, where the subject is named.

comm.t: Biḍāla’s entry is completed, and the roll turns to the many unnamed generals, each with his tens of thousands of chariots, elephants and horses.

The muster-roll is longer in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as preserved in GRETIL, which carries verses here that the Gita Press text does not; the recited Saptaśatī of seven hundred mantras is followed in this edition, and nothing is added to it.

mantras.anvaya: (अन्ये च) महासुराः तत्र संयुगे देव्या सह युयुधुः। (महिषासुरः) तु रथानां दन्तिनां तथा (हयानां च) कोटिकोटिसहस्रैः (2.47: वृतः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the sentence of 2.45b. With तु the second turns to Mahiṣāsura himself; the instrumental and genitives belong with वृतः in 2.47.
mantras.lit: great asuras fought there in the battle with the Goddess. And, by thousands of crores of crores of chariots and likewise of elephants
mantras.tr: fought there in battle against the Goddess. And with thousands upon thousands of crores of chariots and elephants
mantras.tr_note: The second line runs into 2.47, where Mahiṣāsura is named.

comm.t: All the generals together fight the Goddess. Then तु turns to the king himself: Mahiṣāsura’s own forces are counted in ‘thousands of crores of crores’ — a number meant to be beyond counting.

The army grows from tens of thousands to crores of crores while the Goddess remains one. The disproportion is the point of the roll, and it prepares 2.49–50, where she cuts down their weapons ‘as if in play’ (लीलयैव).

mantras.lit: and of horses, surrounded, Mahiṣāsura was there in the battle. With javelins and bhindipālas, with spears and likewise with clubs —
mantras.tr: and horses around him, Mahiṣāsura himself stood in the battle. With javelins and throwing-spears, with lances and clubs
mantras.tr_note: The second line is completed in 2.48 (‘they fought with the Goddess …’).

comm.t: Mahiṣāsura himself is in the field, at the centre of an army counted in crores of crores. The weapon list that follows (javelins, bhindipālas, spears, clubs) begins the asuras’ assault, completed in 2.48.
The bhindipāla, named here among the asuras’ weapons, is also carried by the Goddess’s own attendant hosts (भिन्दिपालासिपट्टिशैः, 2.53) and is the weapon with which she strikes down Bāṣkala (3.18).

morph.note: √युध् is ātmanepadin (युध्यते; perfect युयुधे, as in 2.41 and 2.43). The plural here takes the parasmaipada ending -उः instead of the classical युयुधिरे — the usual epic and Purāṇic form, used again in 2.53 and 2.63.

mantras.anvaya: (ते महासुराः तोमरैः भिन्दिपालैः च शक्तिभिः मुसलैः तथा) खड्गैः परशुपट्टिशैः (च) संयुगे देव्या (सह) युयुधुः। केचित् च शक्तीः चिक्षिपुः, केचित् पाशान् (चिक्षिपुः); तथा अपरे —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence begun in 2.47b (तोमरैः … मुसलैः तथा): the list of instruments runs across the verse boundary. The second line distributes the action: ‘some … some … and others’; अपरे is taken as the subject of 2.49.
mantras.lit: (With lances, javelins, spears and clubs,) with swords, with axes and paṭṭiśas they fought with the Devī in the battle. And some hurled spears, some nooses; and likewise others —
mantras.tr: With lances and javelins, with spears and maces, with swords, axes and halberds, they fought the Goddess in that battle. Some hurled spears, others nooses; and still others —
mantras.tr_note: The opening phrase is carried over from 2.47b. ‘Halberds’ renders पट्टिश loosely. The verse ends on अपरे, whose action follows in 2.49.

comm.t: The asura host, mustered in 2.40–47, attacks all at once. The verse names a whole armoury — swords, axes, paṭṭiśas, spears, nooses — to show the full weight of the assault the Devī is about to cut down.
The weapons the asuras use are largely those the gods have just given the Devī (2.20–31: spear, noose, axe, sword). The battle is fought weapon against weapon, and the text will show hers prevailing.

flags.uncertain: अपरे can also be read within this verse as an elliptical third member (‘and others likewise [hurled other weapons]’). Here it is taken with 2.49, on the pattern of तथापरे in 2.57–58, where the clause clearly runs on.

samasa.alt: Also a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, खड्गेन प्रहाराः ‘blows (dealt) with the sword’; the sense is the same.

चण्डी ‘the fierce (woman)’ with the suffix -क: Caṇḍikā, the name by which the Devī is most often called in the middle and last caritas.

mantras.anvaya: (अपरे) ते तु खड्गप्रहारैः तां देवीं हन्तुं प्रचक्रमुः। ततः सा देवी चण्डिका अपि तानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि (च) —
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences. The first ends the asuras’ assault. The second has its subject (सा देवी चण्डिका) and objects (तानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि) here and its verb (प्रचिच्छेद) in 2.50.
mantras.lit: And they set about to kill her, the Devī, with sword-strokes. She too, the Devī Caṇḍikā, then — those weapons and missiles —
mantras.tr: set out to cut the Goddess down with blows of the sword. Then the Goddess Caṇḍikā, in her turn, took those weapons and missiles —
mantras.tr_note: The second line has no verb of its own; ‘took’ in the readable version only bridges to ‘cut to pieces’ in 2.50, where the verb stands.

comm.t: The attack reaches its height: the asuras close in with swords to kill her. The second line turns at once to the Devī’s answer, which 2.50 completes: she cuts every weapon down.
The pair शस्त्र and अस्त्र is the standard division of weapons: śastra is held and wielded, astra is released — thrown, shot or discharged. Naming both says that no kind of weapon reached her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names her Caṇḍikā (name 755, चण्डिका). In the Devī Māhātmya the name belongs above all to the warrior Goddess of these battle chapters.

mantras.anvaya: (सा देवी चण्डिका तानि शस्त्राणि अस्त्राणि) निजशस्त्रास्त्रवर्षिणी लीलया एव प्रचिच्छेद। अनायस्तानना सुरर्षिभिः स्तूयमाना देवी —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence of 2.49b with its verb प्रचिच्छेद. The second line opens a new sentence whose verb, मुमोच, stands in 2.51.
mantras.lit: Raining her own weapons and missiles, she cut (them) to pieces merely in play. The Devī, her face unwearied, being praised by the gods and seers —
mantras.tr: and, raining down her own weapons and missiles, cut them to pieces as if in play. Unwearied of face, praised by gods and seers, the Goddess —
mantras.tr_note: The verse divides between two sentences; the dash marks the subject of 2.51.

comm.t: The point is effortlessness: लीलया एव ‘merely in play’ and अनायस्तानना ‘her face unstrained’. The whole armoury of 2.48 is undone without the Devī showing effort, while gods and seers look on and praise her.

The same phrase returns in the third carita: Caṇḍikā cuts Śumbha’s weapons चिच्छेद लीलया (8.31). The tradition hears in लीला the Devī’s freedom: what she does in the world is play, not labour or need.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has a close image in its own battle with Bhaṇḍa: name 79, भण्डासुरेन्द्रनिर्मुक्तशस्त्रप्रत्यस्त्रवर्षिणी, ‘she who rains counter-missiles against the weapons released by Bhaṇḍāsura’. Both texts use the same agent noun -वर्षिणी for the warrior Goddess; the battles themselves are different stories.

mantras.lit: the Sovereign released weapons and missiles on the bodies of the asuras. He too, enraged, his mane shaken, the lion that was the Devī’s mount —
mantras.tr: loosed her weapons and missiles upon the asuras’ bodies, sovereign that she is. And her lion too, the Goddess’s own mount, raging and tossing his mane —

comm.t: Defence turns to attack: having destroyed the asuras’ weapons, the Devī now looses her own on their bodies. The lion given her by Himavat (2.29) enters the fight in his own right.
ईश्वरी, ‘sovereign’, is chosen at the moment she goes on the offensive: the battle is the exercise of her lordship, not a contest between equals.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the lion’s sentence from 2.51b, with a simile. The second line is a relative clause (यान् … मुमुचे) whose main clause (ते एव … गणाः) is in 2.53.
mantras.lit: ranged among the asura armies like fire in forests. And the breaths which Ambikā, fighting in battle, released —
mantras.tr: raged through the asura ranks like a fire through the forests. And every breath that Ambikā breathed out as she fought —

comm.t: Two images of the Devī’s power multiplying. The lion goes through the army like a forest fire; and the Devī’s very breathing becomes a weapon, as the next verse shows.

The contrast with Mahiṣa is drawn by the text itself: in the next chapter Mahiṣāsura fells the Devī’s troops with the wind of his breath (निःश्वासपवनेन, 3.23). Her breath brings forth an army; his only destroys.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names her Ambikā (name 295, अम्बिका), ‘the Mother’ — the name the Devī Māhātmya uses most often in its battle scenes.

mantras.lit: those very (breaths) at once became gaṇas by hundreds of thousands. They fought with axes, with javelins, swords and paṭṭiśas,
mantras.tr: became at once her hosts, hundreds of thousands strong. They fought with axes, javelins, swords and halberds,

comm.t: The Devī’s breath becomes an army. She does not summon allies from outside: her own exhalations take form as gaṇas, hundreds of thousands of them, and go into battle with weapons of their own.

The text itself later states the principle behind this: when Śumbha taunts her for relying on others, the Devī answers that she alone is there, and the powers he saw were hers, returning into her (10.5, एकैवाहं जगत्यत्र). The gaṇas here are an early instance: her helpers are her own power.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) likewise gives its Goddess an army that is her own power: name 65, भण्डासुरवधोद्युक्तशक्तिसेनासमन्विता, ‘accompanied by an army of śaktis intent on slaying Bhaṇḍāsura’. The idea is shared; the stories are separate.

mantras.lit: destroying the hosts of the asuras, strengthened by the Devī’s power. (Some) gaṇas sounded war-drums, and likewise others conches,
mantras.tr: destroying the asura hosts, made mighty by the Goddess’s power. Some of the hosts beat the war-drums, others blew the conches,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Beat’ and ‘blew’ render the one verb अवादयन्त ‘sounded’ for each instrument.

comm.t: The gaṇas both fight and make music. Their strength is not their own: it is the Devī’s power (देवीशक्ति) that swells them. Drums and conches are the sounds of an army sure of victory.
A modern reading: the same beings destroy and celebrate in one breath. The text does not separate the battle from the festival — 2.55 will call it a ‘great festival of war’.

comm.t: The orchestra is completed — war-drums, conches, mṛdaṅgas — and the battle is named a ‘great festival’. Then the Devī herself takes up her weapons: the trident, the mace and the spear-showers begin the list that runs into 2.56.
Several of these weapons are the gods’ gifts of 2.20–24: Śiva’s trident, Agni’s śakti, and the sword (2.56) given by Kāla. The armed form the gods made is now at work.

mantras.tr: with sword and every other weapon, struck down the great asuras by the hundred; and others, dazed by the ringing of her bell, she brought to the ground.

comm.t: The Devī’s own slaughter begins. Even her bell is a weapon: its sound stupefies the asuras before they are felled.

The bell is Indra’s gift, taken from Airāvata (2.22). It returns in the gods’ hymn of the eleventh chapter, which asks that the bell that fills the world with its sound and destroys the daityas’ might protect them from sin, as one guards one’s children (11.27).

mantras.anvaya_en: First line: absolutive + finite verb with the Devī as subject. Second: a passive participle as verb with an instrumental of means. अपरे opens the sentence completed in 2.58.
mantras.lit: And binding other asuras with the noose, she dragged (them) on the ground. Some were made in two by sharp sword-strokes; likewise others —
mantras.tr: Others she bound with her noose and dragged along the ground. Some were cut in two by the keen strokes of her sword; and others —
mantras.tr_note: भुवि may also go with बद्ध्वा (‘bound on the ground’); the readable version joins it to the dragging.

comm.t: Each weapon has its own work: the noose binds and drags, the sword cuts in two. The verse begins the catalogue of the asuras’ deaths that runs to 2.64.
The noose is Varuṇa’s gift (2.23). In iconography the pāśa is the binding power that the Goddess holds over those who oppose her.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence has its subject, अपरे, at the end of 2.57. Each clause: participle(s) + instrumental of means + finite verb.
mantras.lit: (others,) crushed by the blow, by the mace, lie on the ground. And some, struck hard by the club, vomited blood.
mantras.tr: others lie on the ground, crushed by the blows of her mace; and some, struck hard by her club, spewed blood.
mantras.tr_note: निपातेन गदया, two instrumentals side by side (‘by the blow, with the mace’), are rendered as one phrase.

comm.t: Two more weapons, two more deaths: the mace crushes, the musala (club) makes the asuras spew blood. The verse moves into the present (शेरते ‘they lie’), as if the narrator were looking at the field.

The mace (गदा) is among the weapons held by Mahālakṣmī in the Gita Press dhyāna for this carita (… गदेषुकुलिशं …); that the middle carita is presided over by Mahālakṣmī is the liturgical tradition of the pāṭha, not a statement of the Purāṇa.

mantras.lit: Some fell on the ground, pierced in the chest by the spear. Some were made gapless by a flood of arrows on the battlefield.
mantras.tr: Some, pierced through the chest by her spear, fell to the ground; some, on the field of battle, were riddled through and through by her storm of arrows.

comm.t: The catalogue continues: the śūla pierces the chest, the arrows leave no space unwounded. निरन्तर, ‘without interval’, pictures bodies covered with arrows from end to end.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete sentence (subject at the end). The second gives two short clauses with the verb ‘to be’ understood.
mantras.lit: The tormentors of the gods, imitating hawks, released their life-breaths. Of some the arms were cut off; likewise others had their necks cut.
mantras.tr: Like hawks dropping from the sky, the tormentors of the gods gave up their lives. Some had their arms hewn off, and others their heads struck from their necks.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Dropping from the sky’ interprets श्येनानुकारिणः ‘imitating hawks’, which the Sanskrit leaves unexplained; see Samāsa for the other construction.

comm.t: The asuras are called त्रिदशार्दनाः, ‘tormentors of the Thirty’, at the moment they die: the epithet recalls why the battle is fought (2.6–8). The second line goes on cataloguing wounds — arms, necks.

flags.uncertain: The point of comparison in श्येनानुकारिणः is not stated: it may describe the asuras (falling as hawks drop) or, as an accusative, their departing breaths (flying off like hawks). Both constructions are recorded; the choice is interpretive.

mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses, each with its own subject: heads fell; others were split; still others fell hamstrung.
mantras.lit: The heads of others fell; others were torn apart in the middle; and other great asuras, their legs cut off, fell on the earth.
mantras.tr: Others’ heads fell; others were split through the middle; and still other great asuras, their legs hewn away, fell to the earth.

comm.t: The anatomy of the slaughter continues — heads, waists, legs. The repetition of पेतुः ‘fell’ frames the verse.
A modern reading: the unflinching detail of these verses is not cruelty for its own sake. The text wants the defeat of what oppresses the gods to be total and visible, limb by limb.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence explains the compound: cut in two, they were left with one arm, eye and foot. The second sentence continues into 2.63, where the risen trunks fight.
mantras.lit: Some, cut in two by the Devī, (were left) with one arm, one eye, one foot. And others, even when the head was cut off, having fallen rose up again.
mantras.tr: Some the Goddess cleft in two, leaving each half one arm, one eye, one foot. And others, though their heads were struck off, fell and rose again —

comm.t: The battle turns grotesque: asuras split lengthwise, and headless bodies that fall and stand up again. The next two verses describe these headless trunks (कबन्ध) fighting on.
Headless trunks (कबन्ध) rising and fighting on are a familiar image in epic battle descriptions. Here it marks the asuras’ ferocity: they resist even past death, and it is still not enough.

mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence continues 2.62b (अन्ये … पुनः उत्थिताः): the risen bodies, now कबन्धाः, fight. The second is parallel: others dance.
mantras.lit: As headless trunks, grasping excellent weapons, they fought with the Devī; and others danced there in the battle, keeping to the rhythm of the instruments.
mantras.tr: and fought the Goddess as headless trunks, still gripping their finest weapons; and others danced there on the battlefield to the beat of the war-music.

comm.t: The headless bodies of 2.62 fight on, and some even dance to the rhythm of the drums and conches the gaṇas are playing (2.54–55). The festival of battle (युद्धमहोत्सव) has its macabre dancers.
A modern reading: what has lost its head can still move to the music of battle. Resistance can go on long after its reason is gone.

mantras.anvaya_en: The verse has no finite verb: the participle भाषन्तः serves as predicate (‘were crying’), or युयुधुः is carried over from 2.63.
mantras.lit: Other great asuras — headless trunks, their heads severed, swords, spears and ṛṣṭis in their hands — (were) saying to the Devī, ‘Stop! Stop!’
mantras.tr: Other great asuras, headless trunks with their heads struck off, swords and spears and lances still in their hands, kept crying to the Goddess, ‘Stand! Stand and fight!’
mantras.tr_note: ‘Kept crying’ supplies the missing finite verb. The headless shout although they have no heads — the text does not explain it, and the translation does not either.

comm.t: The grotesque reaches its climax: headless asuras, still armed, challenge the Devī with the warrior’s cry तिष्ठ तिष्ठ. The image shows a defiance that outlives the body.
The challenge ‘Stop! Stop!’ is the formula of epic combat, addressed to an opponent who is withdrawing or must stand and fight. Here it is spoken by the dead to the one who cannot be stopped.

mantras.lit: By felled chariots, elephants and horses, and by asuras, the earth — it became impassable there, where that great battle took place.
mantras.tr: Where that great battle was fought, the earth became impassable, strewn with fallen chariots, elephants, horses and asuras.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Strewn with’ renders the instrumental of cause (‘by …’).

comm.t: The camera pulls back from single deaths to the whole field: so many chariots, elephants, horses and asuras lie fallen that the ground cannot be crossed.

mantras.anvaya_en: One sentence: subject (शोणितौघाः) with a predicate noun (महानद्यः), place (तत्र … मध्ये with genitives), verb (प्रसुस्रुवुः).
mantras.lit: Torrents of blood, great rivers, at once flowed forth there, in the midst of the asura army, of elephants, asuras and horses.
mantras.tr: At once torrents of blood flowed there like great rivers, through the midst of the asura host, among its elephants, warriors and horses.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Like’ makes explicit the identification of the torrents with great rivers, which the Sanskrit states by apposition.

comm.t: The scale of the slaughter is measured in rivers of blood running through the asura army itself — among its own elephants, warriors and horses.

mantras.anvaya_en: A correlative simile: यथा (the fire) … तथा (Ambikā). The verb of the simile is supplied from निन्ये.
mantras.lit: In a moment Ambikā so led that great army of the asuras to destruction, as fire (does) a great heap of grass and wood.
mantras.tr: In a moment Ambikā brought that vast army of the asuras to ruin, as fire consumes a great heap of straw and timber.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Consumes’ renders the verb supplied in the simile (‘leads to destruction’).

comm.t: The summary verse of the battle: the whole army is gone in a moment (क्षणेन), as easily as fire takes dry fuel. The simile returns to the fire-image used of the lion in 2.52.
A modern reading: the asuras’ vast numbers — tens of thousands of chariots, crores of elephants — are only fuel. Size is no defence against what the text presents as the power of the Goddess.

mantras.anvaya: सः च सिंहः धुतकेसरः महानादम् उत्सृजन् अमरारीणां शरीरेभ्यः असून् विचिन्वति इव।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with two qualifiers (one a participial phrase), then the verb; इव makes the whole action an ‘as it were’.
mantras.lit: And that lion, letting out a great roar, his mane shaking, as it were picks out the life-breaths from the bodies of the enemies of the immortals.
mantras.tr: And the lion, shaking his mane and roaring mightily, ranged as if he were plucking the very lives out of the bodies of the gods’ enemies.
mantras.tr_note: The readable version puts the historic present into the past and adds ‘ranged’ to carry the image; the Sanskrit has only ‘as it were picks out’.

comm.t: The lion returns (2.51–52). He roars and tosses his mane, and moves among the fallen as if searching out any life still left in their bodies — the last stroke of the battle.

The Devī’s lion is more than a mount in the Devī Māhātmya: it fights in its own right here (2.51–52, 2.68), against Mahiṣa’s generals (3.14), against Dhūmralocana’s army (6.15–19) and against Niśumbha’s forces (9.37). It shares in the work of the Goddess who rides it.

flags.uncertain: विचिन्वति is taken as a finite verb (3rd sg. present, thematic ārṣa form). Grammatically it could also be the locative singular of the participle विचिन्वत्, but nothing in the verse agrees with a locative, so that reading does not construe.

morph.note: Impersonal-looking passive: युद्धं कृतम् ‘battle was made’ with the agents in the instrumental (देव्या गणैः च) and the opponents also in the instrumental (महासुरैः). The two instrumentals are told apart by sense.
Perfect of √तुष् with reduplication तु-: ‘they were gratified’.

mantras.anvaya: तत्र देव्या तैः गणैः च महासुरैः (सह) युद्धं (तथा) कृतं, यथा दिवि पुष्पवृष्टिमुचः देवाः एषां तुतुषुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause in the passive (युद्धं कृतम् with instrumental agents), followed by a यथा-clause of result. एषाम् ‘of them’ is a loose genitive of reference: the gods were pleased with them (with the Devī and her gaṇas); it can also be taken with पुष्पवृष्टिमुचः, ‘showering flowers on them’.
mantras.lit: There the battle was waged by the Devī and by those gaṇas with the great asuras in such a way that the gods, releasing rains of flowers in heaven, were pleased with them.
mantras.tr: So the Goddess and her hosts fought the great asuras there, and fought so well that the gods in heaven rejoiced in them and rained down flowers.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Fought so well’ makes explicit the result-clause यथा (‘in such a way that’).

comm.t: The chapter closes on the gods’ response: the battle of the Devī and her gaṇas against the asura champions is such that the gods, watching from heaven, shower flowers. The asura army is destroyed; Mahiṣāsura himself remains for the next chapter (महिषासुरवधः).

The text has a variant here: the Gita Press reads कृतं युद्धं महासुरैः ‘with the great asuras’; GRETIL and Freund read कृतं युद्धं तथासुरैः ‘and likewise with the asuras’ (corrections.json, variants). The sense of the verse is the same. In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter’s last mantra closes with the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the recitation, not to the Purāṇa.

A modern reading: the chapter of slaughter ends not with corpses but with flowers falling from the sky — the gods’ gratitude. The violence is told as the clearing of the way for what the gods could not do for themselves.

flags.uncertain: Variant reading (Textual Verification Required): महासुरैः (Gita Press, kept) against तथासुरैः (GRETIL, Freund). With तथासुरैः the line reads ‘battle was waged by the Devī and her gaṇas, and likewise by the asuras’ or ‘with the asuras likewise’. The construction of एषाम् (with तुतुषुः or with पुष्पवृष्टिमुचः) is also open.
